title: Sort the Olympic Table
constraints: gold_medals, silver_medals and bronze_medals are 0 or more
country names compare without regard to case, as in MySQL
reference:
SELECT country, gold_medals, silver_medals, bronze_medals
FROM Olympic
ORDER BY
  gold_medals DESC,
  silver_medals DESC,
  bronze_medals DESC,
  country ASC;
brute:
SELECT o.country, o.gold_medals, o.silver_medals, o.bronze_medals
FROM Olympic AS o
ORDER BY (
  SELECT COUNT(*)
  FROM Olympic AS b
  WHERE b.gold_medals > o.gold_medals
     OR (b.gold_medals = o.gold_medals AND b.silver_medals > o.silver_medals)
     OR (b.gold_medals = o.gold_medals AND b.silver_medals = o.silver_medals AND b.bronze_medals > o.bronze_medals)
     OR (b.gold_medals = o.gold_medals AND b.silver_medals = o.silver_medals AND b.bronze_medals = o.bronze_medals AND b.country < o.country)
)
notes:
## Intuition

Nothing is filtered or computed: the task is purely about ordering. A medal table compares countries the way a dictionary compares words, one column at a time: gold decides unless it is equal, then silver, then bronze, then the name. `ORDER BY` with several keys does exactly this, consulting each key only when all earlier keys tie.

## Approach

1. `SELECT` the four columns of `Olympic` in their original order.
2. `ORDER BY gold_medals DESC`: more gold first.
3. Add `silver_medals DESC` and `bronze_medals DESC` as the next tie-breakers.
4. Finish with `country ASC` so countries with identical counts come out alphabetically, which makes the order unique.

## Example 1, step by step

- China and USA both have 10 gold, 10 silver and 20 bronze, so the name decides: China before USA.
- Israel and Egypt both have 2 gold and 2 silver; Israel's 3 bronze beat Egypt's 2.
- South Sudan has no gold, so it comes last despite its bronze medal.

Result: China, USA, Israel, Egypt, South Sudan.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n log n) to sort the n countries.
- Space: O(n) for the sorted result.

## Pitfalls

- Leaving out `DESC` sorts ascending, putting the countries with the fewest medals first. `DESC` applies to one key only, so it must be repeated on each medal column.
- Omitting `country` leaves fully tied countries in an arbitrary order, which fails an ordered comparison.
- Ranking by the total number of medals is a different table: one gold outranks any number of silver or bronze medals.

## Clauses

| Name | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `gold_medals DESC` | primary key of the order: more gold first |
| `silver_medals DESC` | used only between countries with equal gold |
| `bronze_medals DESC` | used only when gold and silver are both equal |
| `country ASC` | final tie-break, alphabetical |

narration.1: Return the table as it is: all four columns in their original order.
narration.3: The sort keys follow, each one consulted only when every earlier key ties.
narration.4: Gold decides first: more gold medals rank higher.
narration.5: Between countries with equal gold, more silver ranks higher.
narration.6: Bronze breaks ties that remain after gold and silver.
narration.7: Fully tied countries are listed alphabetically, so the order is unique.
